paper_title: Flip a Failure into a Success: Improved Bit Flipping Decoding for QC-MDPC Codes
authors: Paolo Santini, Davide De Zuane, Alessio Baldelli, and Marco Baldi

statement: In BIKE, decryption failures correspond to decoding failures, that is, events in which the decoder cannot correct the error pattern sampled during encapsulation. Thus, the decryption failure probability corresponds to the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) and IND-CCA2 can be achieved only if the (average) DFR is less than 2´λ . In particular, BIKE employs Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes, for which efficient decoding strategies are intrinsically characterized by some non-zero DFR. To guarantee that the DFR is ă 2´λ , one needs an efficient decoding algorithm with a sound and convincing theoretical assessment about its DFR. Even though, in recent years, a variety of works have studied this topic [2]–[11], arguably, none of these works is a silver bullet and this problem remains open. As highlighted in the NIST report on the fourth round of the standardization process [12], the DFR issue was a relevant obstacle standing between BIKE and its standardization.
context: As a common feature of both BIKE and HQC, decryption may fail even for genuine ciphertexts: this is because the underlying decoder may terminate the decoding process with a failure, and opens up for attacks leveraging decryption queries1 . To achieve INDistinguishability under Adaptively Chosen Ciphertext Attacks (IND-CCA2), the decryption failure probability must be smaller than 2´λ , with λ being the security parameter [1]. In BIKE, decryption failures correspond to decoding failures, that is, events in which the decoder cannot correct the error pattern sampled during encapsulation. Thus, the decryption failure probability corresponds to the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) and IND-CCA2 can be achieved only if the (average) DFR is less than 2´λ . In particular, BIKE employs Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes, for which efficient decoding strategies are intrinsically characterized by some non-zero DFR. To guarantee that the DFR is ă 2´λ , one needs an efficient decoding algorithm with a sound and convincing theoretical assessment about its DFR. Even though, in recent years, a variety of works have studied this topic [2]–[11], arguably, none of these works is a silver bullet and this problem remains open. As highlighted in the NIST report on the fourth round of the standardization process [12], the DFR issue was a relevant obstacle standing between BIKE and its standardization. The remainder of this section introduces, with some more technical details, the QC-MDPC codes used in BIKE, their decoding and the related issues. LDPC, MDPC and BF decoding. MDPC codes are close relatives of Low Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, introduced by Gallager in 1962 [13]. LDPC and MDPC codes admit sparse parity-check matrices, that is, matrices where rows and columns have low Hamming weight. For MDPC codes, parity-check matrices are somewhat denser than those of LDPC codes2 .
